intro.title: Say what you need
paragraphs: For the last few weeks you and your partner have barely spent time together. You want to change that, but the talk could turn into reproaches.
You try to talk about your need, not about their fault.
Choose what to say. If an answer doesn’t work, you stay where you are, see the reaction and understand why.
intro.note: The other person’s styles are patterns of behaviour, not types of people: the same person acts differently on different days. Real people react differently, so this is practice with wording, not a prediction.
intro.disclaimer: A learning simulation. The material draws on well-known communication methods (sources are given at each step), but it has not yet been reviewed by a psychologist.

variants.name: Tired and closed off
variants.desc: Comes home drained, answers briefly, wants things “to the point”.

variants.name: Touchy
variants.desc: Quickly hears blame and gets upset.

nodes.narr: Late evening at home. For the last few weeks you’ve barely spent time together, and it has become hard. You want to say so.

options.text: I’d like to talk about us, without reproaches. When suits you: ten minutes tonight or at the weekend?
options.why: A soft start with a choice of time reduces the feeling of being attacked. You’re not accusing, you’re inviting a conversation.

direct.say: Let’s do the weekend, I have no energy today. Thanks for not making it tonight.

evasive.say: OK, let’s do the weekend. I need to prepare.

options.text: You don’t care about me at all!
options.why: The sentence starts with “you” and sounds like an accusation. The other person defends themselves, and the topic of your need gets lost.

direct.say: That’s unfair, I’m working myself to death.

evasive.say: So I’m bad? That’s it, I don’t want to hear this.

options.text: Nothing, I just wanted to sit together.
options.why: The need is named too vaguely and without a reason. The other person doesn’t understand what the talk is about.

direct.say: OK, let’s sit. Did something happen?

evasive.say: Let’s sit… is something wrong?

options.text: Oh, nothing, some other time.
options.why: Postponing without a date means bottling it up. What’s unsaid will grow and burst out at an awkward moment.

direct.say: OK, as you like.

evasive.say: Well, OK.

tech.name: A soft start
tech.text: Start with a description and an invitation, not with criticism and “you always…”.

nodes.hint: How to invite a conversation without opening it as a complaint?

direct.say: I’m very tired today. Is it urgent?

evasive.say: Do you need to discuss something? Sounds serious…

nodes.narr: The other person agreed to listen.
nodes.ask: How do you talk about what you feel?

options.text: For the last few weeks we’ve barely seen each other in the evenings, and I miss it. I’d like us to spend at least a couple of hours a week together.
options.why: The structure: observation, feeling, need, request. You talk about yourself and name something specific instead of blaming.

direct.say: I see. I really didn’t notice how rarely.

evasive.say: OK. It matters to me that you’re saying this.

options.text: You never have time, you never think about me.
options.why: Words like “always” and “never” are generalisations. The other person hears blame and starts listing exceptions.

direct.say: Not true. Last week we went to the cinema.

evasive.say: Right now it hurts to hear “never”.

options.text: I’m just sad, that’s all.
options.why: Describing a feeling without an observation and a request leaves the other person guessing. They don’t know what to do.

direct.say: So what am I supposed to do now?

evasive.say: I’m sad too… but what do we do about it?

options.text: Other couples are together all the time.
options.why: Comparing with others makes people feel inadequate and leads to an argument.

direct.say: Then go live with those others.

evasive.say: OK, so I’m worse than others.

tech.name: Observation, feeling, need, request
tech.text: Talk about what you see and feel and ask for a specific action.

nodes.hint: How to talk about your need without blaming?

direct.say: Go on then. Just to the point.

evasive.say: OK… I’m listening.

nodes.narr: The other person answers, and you can hear tiredness in it.

options.text: You get really tired, and you need quiet after work. That makes sense. I want to find a way that works for both of us.
options.why: Validation shows you heard and accepted the other person’s position. The solution is looked for together.

direct.say: Thanks for understanding. Let’s figure something out.

evasive.say: It’s easier for me when you say it like that. Let’s figure something out.

options.text: But I get tired too, and I still find the energy.
options.why: Comparing tiredness devalues the other person’s experience and starts a “who has it harder” argument.

direct.say: Don’t compare, it’s unfair.

evasive.say: So I’m weak.

options.text: OK, forget it, this talk was pointless.
options.why: Backing off at the first objection shuts down your need and leaves resentment.

direct.say: OK, forgotten.

evasive.say: Fine, forgotten, as you say.

options.text: Just go to bed earlier, that’s all.
options.why: Unrequested advice comes across as brushing off feelings.

direct.say: Thanks for the advice.

evasive.say: I don’t need advice.

tech.name: Validation
tech.text: Show that you understand the other person’s feelings and reasons, without agreeing with everything or arguing.

nodes.hint: How to show you heard their tiredness?

direct.say: I really am worn out. After work I need some quiet.

evasive.say: I’m trying. And you’re complaining on top of it…

nodes.narr: The tension has eased. Time to suggest something specific.

options.text: Let’s try this: two evenings a week, an hour each without phones, and leave the other evenings as they are. Does that work?
options.why: A small realistic experiment is easier to accept than “always together”. You ask for something specific and leave a choice.

direct.say: Two evenings, an hour each… that’s doable. Let’s try.

evasive.say: OK, an hour on two evenings. That’s not scary.

options.text: I want us to spend every evening together.
options.why: A request that’s too big causes resistance. The other person feels they won’t manage.

direct.say: Every evening? That’s impossible.

evasive.say: Every evening? I’ll suffocate.

options.text: Well, somehow more time.
options.why: A vague request makes it impossible to agree and check whether it’s been done.

direct.say: More — how much is that?

evasive.say: Somehow… that’s nothing.

options.text: Either this, or I’ll understand you don’t need this relationship.
options.why: An ultimatum plays on fear and closes the dialogue.

direct.say: Don’t blackmail me.

evasive.say: You can’t do that, you’re scaring me.

tech.name: A small specific request
tech.text: Ask for a specific action of a clear size: when, how long, how often.

nodes.hint: What request is easy to do and easy to check?

direct.say: So what do you want?

evasive.say: OK. What exactly are you suggesting?

nodes.narr: An agreement is close. It’s important to end warmly.

options.text: Thank you for listening and looking for a solution. It means a lot to me. Let’s check in two weeks how it’s going.
options.why: Thanks for something specific and a promise to check after a set time turn the agreement into a living process. You value the effort, not just the result.

direct.say: Yes, let’s. It matters to me too.

evasive.say: OK, we’ll check. Thank you.

options.text: You see, nothing terrible.
options.why: A triumphant tone devalues the other person’s feelings and sounds like “I told you so”.

direct.say: Don’t overdo it, OK?

evasive.say: I didn’t say it was terrible.

options.text: I know everything will be fine with us.
options.why: A general reassurance without a plan sounds empty and doesn’t ease anxiety.

direct.say: I hope so.

evasive.say: I hope so…

options.text: OK.
options.why: A short agreement without thanks or a date leaves the feeling the conversation isn’t finished.

direct.say: Well, OK.

evasive.say: OK…

tech.name: Thanks and a check-in
tech.text: Thank them for a specific effort and set a date to check the result.

nodes.hint: How to finish so you support the effort and lock in the agreement?

direct.say: OK. Let’s try.

evasive.say: Fine. We’ll try.

direct.say: OK. Let’s check in two weeks.

evasive.say: OK. Thanks for talking about this.

finale.title: Speak and be heard
finale.lead: The need was named, the tiredness was heard, a small plan was found. Here’s what it relied on:
carry: Starting with an invitation, not a reproach.
Talking about yourself: what I see, what I feel, what I ask.
Asking for something small and specific; thanking them for the effort.
finale.prompt: What do you need from someone close to you? Write it as one sentence: “I’d like…”.
